opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really useful lens, and it maps surprisingly well onto how we're building robot foundation models.

So System 1, in Kahneman's framing, is the fast, intuitive, almost subconscious thinking. For a robot, that's the low-level motor control: how do I move my fingers to grasp this cup, how do I keep my balance when I'm walking on uneven ground. You don't deliberate about that. When you pick up a pen, you're not thinking, "Now I'll rotate my wrist fifteen degrees." It just happens. And that loop has to run very fast, hundreds of times a second, because physics doesn't wait for you.

System 2 is the slow, deliberate reasoning and planning. "I want to make breakfast, so first I open the fridge, find the eggs, then get a pan." That's where the large vision-language models come in. They've absorbed a huge amount of common sense from internet-scale data, so they're quite good at taking an instruction, looking at a scene, and breaking a task into steps.

The interesting part is how you connect the two. In our work on humanoid foundation models, we've explicitly used this dual-system design. A vision-language model, the System 2, runs at a slower rate, maybe around ten hertz, and interprets the scene and the language instruction. It then produces a representation that conditions a System 1 action model, something like a diffusion transformer, which generates smooth, high-frequency motor actions in real time.

The reason I like this framing is that it reflects a real engineering constraint. You can't run a multi-billion-parameter reasoning model at a kilohertz on a robot's onboard compute, and you don't need to. A human doesn't re-plan their entire day each time they take a step. So you split the problem: think slowly where it pays off, react quickly where it's required.

Over time I expect the boundary to blur. Ideally it becomes one model that learns when to think fast and when to think slow, the way humans fluidly move between the two. But right now, the dual-system architecture is a very practical way to get robots that are both smart and physically capable.

r001.rationale: It explicitly maps System 1 to low-level motor control, including grasping and balance.

r002.rationale: It maps System 2 to slow, deliberate reasoning and planning, describing it as the robot’s higher-level task reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I love that framework, because I think it maps onto robotics almost perfectly, maybe better than it maps onto language models.

So in Kahneman's book, system one is the fast, intuitive, almost unconscious part of cognition. You see a ball coming at you, you catch it. You don't think about it. And system two is the slow, deliberate, reasoning part. Planning a trip, doing a math problem, deciding how to break a complicated task into steps.

In robotics, system one is the low-level control. It's the thing that runs at a hundred or a thousand hertz, that keeps a humanoid balanced, that closes the fingers around a cup without crushing it. It has to be fast, it has to be reactive, and it has to be incredibly robust, because if it fails, the robot falls over. And interestingly, that's the part that humans find trivial and that robots find really hard. This is the classic Moravec's paradox. Walking is easy for a toddler and painfully hard for a machine.

System two is the high-level reasoning. Understand what the human actually wants, look at the scene, figure out that making coffee means first opening the cabinet, then grabbing the mug, then operating the machine. That's where the big foundation models come in. Language models and vision-language models are, in a sense, system two engines. They're slow, maybe a few tokens a second, but they can reason about the world in a very general way.

The way I think about building a robot brain is you want both, and you want them to talk to each other at the right frequency. The system two model sits on top, runs at a low rate, maybe once a second or slower, and produces a plan or an intermediate representation. The system one policy sits underneath, runs at high frequency, and turns that into motor commands. And the key is you don't want to collapse them into one thing, because the requirements are genuinely different. One needs breadth and reasoning, the other needs speed and physical precision.

What's exciting to me is that for a long time system two for robots basically didn't exist. We had controllers, we had a little bit of task planning, but no general reasoning. Now we have it, almost for free, from the language model world. So the bottleneck has flipped. The hard part today is system one. How do you learn a controller that's as general as the planner on top of it? And my bet is that the answer looks a lot like what happened with language: massive amounts of data, in this case from simulation, from teleoperation, from video, and a model that learns the physics intuition the way a child does, by just doing a lot of things in a lot of worlds.

So the framework isn't just a metaphor for me. It's basically the architecture diagram.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes system one in robotics as low-level control that runs quickly and reactively, producing motor commands.

r002.rationale: It identifies system two as slow, deliberate reasoning and maps it to high-level robotic reasoning and planning.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful way to think about the architecture of a robot. System two is the slower, deliberate part: understanding what you want, reasoning about the world, and breaking a task into steps. System one is the fast, reactive part that actually controls the body.

So if I ask a robot to make coffee, system two might figure out where the mug is, where the coffee machine is, and what order things need to happen in. But when the robot reaches for the mug, you don’t want it reasoning in language about every tiny movement of its fingers. It needs a motor policy that responds quickly to what it sees and feels—especially if the mug slips or somebody bumps its arm.

The interesting challenge is connecting those two systems. A high-level plan has to be grounded in what the robot can actually do, and the motor system has to feed information back when something goes wrong. If the mug is out of reach, the planner needs to adapt.

And I wouldn’t take the analogy too literally. It’s a useful design framework, but it doesn’t necessarily mean you need exactly two models. The core idea is that reasoning and physical control operate at different timescales, and a capable robot needs both.

r001.rationale: It describes system one as the fast, reactive part that controls the robot’s body, including its motor policy.

r002.rationale: It describes system two as the slower, deliberate part that reasons about the world and breaks tasks into steps.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful way to separate two very different problems in robotics. System two is the slower, deliberate part: understanding a goal, reasoning about what needs to happen, and breaking it into steps. If I ask a robot to make coffee, that system might figure out that it needs to find a cup, put it under the machine, and press the right button.

System one is what makes those steps physically happen. How do you reach for the cup? How do you adjust your grip when it starts slipping? You don’t want the robot reasoning in language about every tiny movement. You want a fast policy that maps what it senses into actions, almost like muscle memory.

The interesting challenge is connecting them. A language model can propose a perfectly reasonable plan that the robot can’t actually execute. So the slower system needs feedback from the faster system: Is this reachable? Did the grasp work? Has something changed?

And the distinction isn’t necessarily two separate models. It’s two kinds of computation operating at different timescales. Ultimately, you want a robot that can deliberate when it encounters something unfamiliar, but act fluidly when it knows what to do.

r001.rationale: It describes system one as the fast policy that maps sensory input to physical actions, including reaching and adjusting a grip.

r002.rationale: It describes system two as the slower, deliberate process of understanding goals, reasoning, and breaking tasks into steps.
